newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS - Kodak reports lower earnings, blames dollar.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Kodak reports lower earnings, blames dollar.

text.p: Eastman Kodak Co. said Tuesday its profits fell to $149 million in the first quarter as sales were hurt by the strong dollar, and the photographic and imaging products giant called the results unsatisfactory.

"Overall, 1997 started more slowly than we expected and the first-quarter results are unsatisfactory," Kodak Chairman George Fisher said in a statement. "We need to improve our execution to achieve results which reflect the company's true potential."
But the numbers were not as bad as some analysts had feared, and Wall Street reacted favorably to the report. Kodak stock rose $2.25 to $75.375 in consolidated trading on the New York Stock Exchange.

The first-quarter net income of $149 million, or 45 cents a share, included a pretax charge of $186 million for research and development related to Kodak's acquisition of Wang Laboratories' software business unit.

Excluding the acquisition-related charge, the Rochester, N.Y.-based company's earnings were $272 million, or 80 cents per share, compared with $274 million, or 80 cents a share, in the year-ago quarter.
The consensus analyst forecast was for 81 cents per share, according to First Call, which tracks analyst predictions.
Wall Street had been braced for the worst after Kodak issued a grim sales assessment last month that pushed its stock down $9.75 in a day to $78.50. Analysts were relieved by Tuesday's news.
"I would say the reaction was 'Thank God, it wasn't worse,'" Prudential Securities analyst Alex Henderson said. "There was a lot of concern it could be an ugly quarter."
Quarterly sales, which also were hurt by lower prices, fell to $3.13 billion from $3.39 billion.
Kodak Chief Financial Officer Harry Kavetas said the strong dollar hurt quarterly sales to the tune of about $90 million.
"Without the adverse effect of foreign currency, sales would have increased by 5 percent," the company said. A stronger dollar makes overseas sales worth less in dollar terms.
Taking currency issues into account, sales were flat in January and February but were up 5 percent in March, Kavetas said in an interview.
Kavetas said he doubts the dollar will remain as strong as it is. At current levels, the annualized effect on Kodak sales would be about $500 million, he said.
"If the dollar stays as strong as it is right now ... that exchange rate will continue to produce some pretty significant results," he said.
Kavetas said a "significant slowdown" in emerging markets continued in March. But Kodak said it believed emerging markets will be a source of long-term growth in the future.
Sales of commercial imaging products like copiers were down 16 percent to $1.64 billion. Consumer imaging product sales were $1.5 billion, up 3 percent from a year ago.
Another weak spot was sales of Kodak's Ektacolor photo paper, which shrank 2 percent to 4 percent worldwide and dropped 16 percent to 23 percent in the United States.
An industry source familiar with Kodak said domestic Ektacolor sales dropped partly because Fuji Photo Film Co. Ltd. won an account with Wal-Mart Stores Inc..
Overall camera sales rose between 5 percent and 7 percent worldwide and increased 24 percent to 31 percent in the United States. Outside the United States, camera sales were about even.
